## Choose your tools

We recommend **Python** for the labs. It is the language used in the provided
notebooks and the one we can best help you with. You may use another language or
tool if you prefer, but our examples and support will focus on Python.

Each lab has a Jupyter notebook (`.ipynb`) that you can download. You can work
on it locally on your computer or upload it to **Google Colab** and work in your
browser.


## Option 1: Work locally

For local Python work, we recommend [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) for package
and environment management. You can use another setup if you already have one
you are comfortable with.

Install uv using the [official installation
instructions](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/). Then
create a uv project directory for your lab work and start [JupyterLab](https://jupyterlab.readthedocs.io/en/latest/jupyter):



```bash
uv init sdm_labs
cd sdm_labs
uv add jupyterlab
uv run jupyter lab
```

Another good option for working with notebooks is [VS
Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/datascience/jupyter-notebooks).


```bash
code .
```

Download the lab notebook into this folder and open it in JupyterLab or VS Code.
In VS Code make sure to select the correct Jupyter kernel which by default will
be located in the directory `$proj_dir/.venv`. Install any packages required by
the individual lab into the same environment, for example:

```bash
uv add numpy pandas matplotlib
```

Those packages are examples; follow each lab's instructions for what you
actually need. Keep any supplied data files in the locations expected by the
notebook.


## Option 2: Work in Google Colab

[Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/) lets you work with Python
notebooks without setting up a local Python environment. Additionally it gives
you access to (limited) GPU resources, which can become relevant in the text and
image analysis part of the course.

1. Download the notebook for the lab.
2. Open Colab, sign in, and use **File → Upload notebook** to open it.
3. Install any additional packages and upload any data files required by the lab, following its instructions.
4. Add your code and written answers directly in the notebook.
5. Save your work and download the completed notebook using **File → Download → Download .ipynb**.

Keep a saved copy of your work. Files uploaded to a Colab runtime are temporary;
you may need to upload data and install additional packages again when starting
a new session.

## Present your answers in the notebook

We expect you to present **both prose and code in the notebook**:

- Use **Markdown cells** for explanations, reasoning, interpretations, and answers to written questions.
- Use **code cells** for calculations, analysis, and visualizations.
- Include the relevant outputs and figures so your reasoning is easy to follow.

Aim for a notebook that reads as a coherent explanation of your work. Explain
what you did, why you did it, and what the results mean.

Before presenting or submitting your work, restart the kernel and run all cells
in order. Check that the notebook works from a fresh session, then save it with
its outputs included. Follow any additional presentation or submission
instructions given for the lab.
